newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left lashes out at Chirac criticisms.
newsitem.headline: French left lashes out at Chirac criticisms.

text.p: French Leftist leaders accused conservative President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday of acting like a political boss rather than a head of state in a televised critique of France's new leftist government.
"He showed that he wanted to take on the role of opposition leader rather than that of president," said Socialist Party head Francois Hollande.
"He was so eager to express his differences that he criticised not only decisions that have been taken but some that have not yet been made," Hollande said on Radio Monte Carlo.

Chirac, in a traditional broadcast appearance on France's July 14 national day, criticised the policies of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on privatisation, layoffs, nuclear power, European unity and immigration.

In his first television interview since being shorn of much of his power by a left-wing victory in parliamentary elections six weeks ago, Chirac said he sought "constructive cohabitation" with Jospin.

But he asserted a broad role for himself that went well beyond the traditional presidential domains of defence and foreign affairs to monitoring the transition to a single European currency, maintaining social cohesion and upholding France's high-technology industries.
Leading leftists said they were dismayed not only by the breadth of his criticisms but their timing as they fell just six weeks after the left took power from the previous centre-right government.

"At this stage, he should have stayed aloof from day-to-day politics, he should have remained the president of all the French but he didn't," said Jack Lang, head of the National Assembly's foreign affairs committee.
The president's words "marked him as the opposition's leading figure," Lang said.
Hollande said the president's message was driven by fear of losing control over his own political apparatus, the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) party which Chirac founded in 1976.

"One might say that he wanted to intrude into the domain of opposition leader for fear he could no longer play that role," Hollande said. referring to former National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin's election as RPR leader earlier this month.
The rotund Seguin, 54, is one of France's most popular political figures and is widely viewed as a potential rival to Chirac when his seven-year presidential term ends in 2002.
Hollande said Chirac's remarks had fallen short of damaging relations with the new government but it was now up to the president to show a willingess to be constructive.
"I think the direction is clear: The government sets policy while the president is the guardian of our institutions. And I think we should continue to maintain this balance," he said.
Asked if he agreed that it was up to the president to assure France's transition to a single European currency, Hollande said the decision would be up to the government and to parliament.
"I believe that we will have to base our decision on the interests of the country," he said.

Asked whether the new government would carry out tax cuts promised by the previous rightist government led by ex-prime minister Alain Juppe, Hollande said reductions favouring only the wealthy would be dropped in favour of a leftist plan to reduce the value-added tax on basic goods.
